commandWords.means: Work out a numerical answer using given data and an equation.
commandWords.doThis: Write the equation, substitute values with units, show working line by line, and give a final answer with the correct unit.

commandWords.means: Use given information or a graph to establish a value or relationship.
commandWords.doThis: Show the reading taken from data or graph and the steps used to reach the value.

commandWords.means: State what happens, in order, without explaining why.
commandWords.doThis: Give a sequence of observations or steps using correct physics vocabulary, no reasoning needed.

commandWords.means: Give reasons or a mechanism, using physics to justify why something happens.
commandWords.doThis: Link cause to effect using connectives like 'because' or 'this means', referencing a physics idea each time.

commandWords.means: Weigh up evidence or a method and reach a justified conclusion.
commandWords.doThis: Give points for and against, refer to the data or method given, then state a supported judgement.

commandWords.means: Give an approximate value using reasonable assumptions.
commandWords.doThis: State the assumption or approximate figure used, then calculate using it, showing working.

commandWords.means: Mark points accurately on a grid from a data table.
commandWords.doThis: Use a sensible scale that fills the grid, plot each point as a small clear cross, do not force through the origin.

commandWords.means: Draw the general shape of a graph without plotting exact points.
commandWords.doThis: Show the correct shape, intercepts and trend; label axes but do not add a scale unless asked.

commandWords.means: Apply physics knowledge to a new or unfamiliar situation.
commandWords.doThis: There may be more than one accepted answer; use physics principles you know and apply them logically to the context given.

commandWords.means: Identify similarities and differences between two things.
commandWords.doThis: Write direct comparative sentences using words like 'whereas' or 'both', covering at least one similarity and one difference.

commandWords.means: Use evidence or physics reasoning to support a statement or choice.
commandWords.doThis: State the claim, then give the physics reason or data point that supports it directly.

commandWords.means: Prove a given value is correct by full calculation.
commandWords.doThis: Write the equation, substitute, calculate to one more significant figure than the target, and compare to the given value.

sections.title: Equations you must recall from memory
sections.note: These 21 equations are NOT printed on the exam paper. Higher tier AQA Physics 8463.

items.detail: W = m x g (weight in N, mass in kg, gravitational field strength in N/kg). Use for any object resting, hanging or falling near Earth.
W = F x d (work in J, force in N, distance in m, along the line of action of the force). Use whenever a force moves something.
F = k x e (force in N, spring constant in N/m, extension in m). Use for springs within their limit of proportionality.
M = F x d (moment in Nm, force in N, perpendicular distance in m). Use for levers, spanners, balancing problems.
v = s / t (speed in m/s, distance in m, time in s). Use for constant speed or to find average speed.
a = (v - u) / t (acceleration in m/s^2, final velocity v, initial velocity u in m/s, time in s). Use whenever velocity changes over time.
F = m x a (force in N, mass in kg, acceleration in m/s^2). Use to link a resultant force to acceleration.
p = m x v (momentum in kg m/s, mass in kg, velocity in m/s). Use for collisions, explosions and conservation of momentum questions.
Ek = 1/2 x m x v^2 (energy in J, mass in kg, speed in m/s). Use for a moving object's energy store.
Ep = m x g x h (energy in J, mass in kg, g in N/kg, height in m). Use for height changes near Earth's surface.
Ee = 1/2 x k x e^2 (energy in J, spring constant in N/m, extension in m). Use only within the limit of proportionality.
P = E / t or P = W / t (power in W, energy or work in J, time in s). Use for rate of energy transfer or rate of doing work.
efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer (no unit, or x100 for percent). Use to compare useful vs wasted energy.
v = f x lambda (speed in m/s, frequency in Hz, wavelength in m). Use for any wave, including sound and light.
Q = I x t (charge in coulombs, current in amps, time in s). Use whenever current flows for a given time.
E = Q x V (energy in J, charge in C, potential difference in V). Use for energy transferred by charge moving through a component.
rho = m / V (density in kg/m^3, mass in kg, volume in m^3). Required practical equation for regular and irregular solids and liquids.
s = v x t. Use to find distance when speed is constant and time is known.
P = F / A (pressure in Pa, force in N, area in m^2). Use for a solid pressing on a surface, not for fluids.
Delta E = m x c x Delta theta (energy in J, mass in kg, specific heat capacity in J/kg degC, temperature change in degC). Use when temperature changes but no state change occurs.

items.term: Energy for a change of state
items.detail: E = m x L (energy in J, mass in kg, specific latent heat in J/kg). Use only during melting/freezing or boiling/condensing, when temperature stays constant.

sections.title: Equations given on the AQA physics equation sheet
sections.note: Printed on the exam paper insert. You still must know when to use each one and be able to rearrange it.

items.detail: F = B x I x l (force in N, magnetic flux density in T, current in A, length in m). Use for motor effect problems.
Vp / Vs = np / ns (primary/secondary potential difference in V, primary/secondary turns). Use for step-up/step-down transformer questions.

items.term: Force on a wire in a field (Alt)
items.detail: Given on sheet alongside motor effect; combine with F=BIl for full circuit and field questions.
Orbital relationships for period and speed are given as descriptive relationships, not a single recalled equation; use given data in the question.
When weight is already given rather than mass and g separately, the sheet shows Ep = weight x height for direct substitution.
n = sin(angle of incidence) / sin(angle of refraction). Use for light passing between two media in required practical work.
T = 1 / f (period in s, frequency in Hz). Given alongside wave speed equation; use to link period and frequency.
P = V x I and P = I^2 x R, both given on sheet. Use P=VI when V and I are known; use I^2R when current and resistance are known and V is not.
F = (m x delta v) / t (force in N, change in momentum in kg m/s, time in s). Use for impact/safety questions like airbags and seatbelts.
For an object in a circular orbit, v = (2 x pi x r) / T (speed in m/s, radius in m, time period T in s). Given on sheet for space physics questions.
Metre, m. All distances must be converted to metres before substituting into equations.
Kilogram, kg. Convert grams to kilograms by dividing by 1000 before using force, energy or momentum equations.
Second, s. Convert minutes and hours to seconds (x60, x3600) before substituting.
Ampere, A.
Kelvin, K, for gas law work; Celsius, degC, for heat capacity/latent heat. To convert: K = degC + 273.
Newton, N, equals kg m/s^2.
Joule, J, equals kg m^2/s^2 or N m.
Watt, W, equals J/s.
Pascal, Pa, equals N/m^2.
Hertz, Hz, equals 1/s (cycles per second).
Coulomb, C, equals A x s.
Divide by 100. 15 cm = 0.15 m. Always convert before substituting into any equation - a very common lost mark.
Divide by 1000. 25 mm = 0.025 m.
Divide by 1000. 250 g = 0.25 kg.

Measure mass, apply known current/voltage to a heater in the material, record temperature rise over time. Independent: energy supplied; dependent: temperature change. Examiners want insulation to reduce heat loss to surroundings noted as a key limitation.

Compare temperature of water in beakers wrapped in different insulating materials over time. Independent: insulating material; dependent: temperature drop. Control the starting temperature and volume of water.

Measure mass with a balance; measure volume by dimensions (regular solid) or displacement (irregular solid/liquid). Calculate density = mass / volume. Examiners want correct handling of water displacement for irregular shapes.
Vary length of wire in circuit, measure current and potential difference, calculate resistance = V / I. Independent: wire length; dependent: resistance. Keep wire diameter and material constant.

Vary potential difference across a resistor, filament lamp and diode, measure current, plot I-V graphs. Examiners want the differences in graph shape explained (resistor = straight line, filament = curves as it heats, diode = only conducts one way).

items.term: RP6: Waves in a solid/spring and in water
items.detail: Measure wavelength and frequency of waves on a stretched string or ripple tank, calculate speed = f x lambda. Independent: frequency; dependent: wavelength measured with a ruler/strobe method.

Use a Leslie cube with different surfaces (matt black, shiny) and an infrared detector to compare emission; also compare absorption using temperature probes. Examiners want the link between surface type and emitter/absorber efficiency.

items.term: RP8: Force and extension of a spring
items.detail: Add masses to a spring, measure extension with a ruler, plot force against extension to find the spring constant from the gradient, and identify the limit of proportionality. Independent: force added; dependent: extension.

Use light gates or a ramp and trolley to measure velocity at two points and time between them, calculate acceleration = change in velocity / time. Independent: ramp angle or force; dependent: acceleration.

items.term: RP10: Frequency of a wave using an oscilloscope
items.detail: Use an oscilloscope trace to read time period from the screen scale, then calculate frequency = 1 / T. Examiners want correct reading of the time-base scale in seconds per division.
The energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius (unit J/kg degC).
The energy required to change the state of one kilogram of a substance with no change in temperature (unit J/kg).
The energy needed to change one kilogram of a substance from solid to liquid at its melting point, with no temperature change.
The energy needed to change one kilogram of a substance from liquid to gas at its boiling point, with no temperature change.
The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles that make up a system.
Force acting normally (at right angles) per unit area: P = F / A, measured in pascals.
-273 degC (0 K), the temperature at which particles have minimum kinetic energy and gas pressure would theoretically reach zero.
A neutral particle with a small, dense, positively charged nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons in shells; atomic radius about 1 x 10^-10 m, nuclear radius about 1 x 10^-14 m.
Atoms of the same element (same proton number) with a different number of neutrons, so a different mass number.
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms it passes through, creating ions.
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays, measured in becquerels (Bq), where 1 Bq = 1 decay per second.
The number of decays recorded per unit time by a detector, e.g. a Geiger-Muller tube; it is proportional to activity but not identical to it because not all decays are detected.
The time taken for the number of nuclei of the original isotope in a sample to halve, or for the count rate/activity from a sample to fall to half its initial level.
The process of exposing an object to radiation from a source; the object does not become radioactive itself.
The unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or in another material, which can then continue to emit radiation from within or on that material.

sections.title: National Grid and energy resources fact bank

items.detail: A system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers, distributing electrical power efficiently around the country.
For a fixed power, higher transmission voltage means lower current; since power loss to heat in cables is I^2 x R, lower current greatly reduces energy wasted.
Located at the power station; increases voltage and decreases current for efficient transmission.
Located near consumers (local substations); decreases voltage to a safe, usable level, e.g. 230 V mains in the UK.
Wind, solar, geothermal, hydroelectric, tidal, wave and biofuel; resources that are replenished as they are used, at a rate comparable to consumption.
Coal, oil, natural gas, nuclear fuel; resources that will eventually run out because they form far slower than they are used.
Turbines convert kinetic energy of moving air into electrical energy; no fuel cost or pollution, but unreliable and can spoil the landscape.
Photovoltaic cells convert light directly into electricity; reliable in daylight, no pollution when running, but output is low on cloudy days or at night.
Water stored in a reservoir is released through turbines; reliable and quick to respond to demand, but has high initial environmental and construction impact.
Uses the rise and fall of tides to drive turbines; predictable timing but not constant power, and can affect estuary ecosystems.
Uses fission of uranium or plutonium to heat water and drive turbines; low running carbon emissions but produces radioactive waste and has high decommissioning costs.
Coal, oil and gas release energy on combustion; reliable and high output, but release carbon dioxide (contributing to global warming) and other pollutants.
Increasing use of renewables and gas, decreasing use of coal, aiming to reduce carbon dioxide emissions over time.
Power stations must be able to respond quickly to changes in demand; pumped storage hydroelectric schemes provide rapid-response backup.
After n half-lives, the fraction remaining is (1/2)^n, not 1/(2n). E.g. after 3 half-lives, 1/8 remains, not 1/6.
A detector only records a fraction of decays (not all radiation reaches it or is detected), so measured count rate underestimates true activity; do not treat them as numerically equal.

items.term: Forgetting to convert cm to m
items.detail: Any length in cm or mm must be converted to metres before use in an equation - a very common lost mark, especially in density, pressure and wave speed questions.
Mass (kg) is constant; weight (N) depends on gravitational field strength and changes with location. Do not use the same number for both without converting via W = m x g.

Distance is total path length (scalar); displacement is straight-line distance from start to finish in a given direction (vector). Area under a speed-time graph gives distance, not displacement, unless direction is tracked.

items.term: Gradient vs area under graph confusion
items.detail: On a distance-time graph, the gradient gives speed. On a velocity-time graph, the gradient gives acceleration AND the area under the graph gives distance travelled - do not mix these up.
In alpha decay, mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number by 2; in beta decay, mass number is unchanged and atomic number increases by 1. Check both numbers balance on each side of the equation.
Do not give a final answer to more significant figures than the least precise piece of data in the question; also do not round intermediate steps too early as this introduces error.

items.term: Confusing energy stores with types of energy
items.detail: AQA uses 'energy stores' (kinetic, thermal, chemical, elastic potential, gravitational potential, nuclear, magnetic, electrostatic) and 'energy transfers' (mechanically, electrically, by heating, by radiation) as separate categories - do not mix the two lists.
A resultant force of zero does not mean no forces act; it means the forces are balanced. Always state 'resultant force' rather than just 'force' in an explanation.
If a calculated efficiency is greater than 1, an error has been made - check which energy value was used as the numerator versus denominator.
In series: current is the same everywhere, potential differences add up. In parallel: potential difference is the same across each branch, currents add up. Mixing these up is a frequent error.
Isolate the unknown algebraically first, e.g. from Q = I x t, to find t: t = Q / I. Only substitute numbers after rearranging to reduce errors.
From Ek = 1/2 x m x v^2, to find v: v = sqrt((2 x Ek) / m). Remember to take the square root as the last step, applied to the whole right-hand side.
Write numbers as A x 10^n where 1 <= A < 10. E.g. 0.00034 = 3.4 x 10^-4; 250000 = 2.5 x 10^5. Use for very large or very small physics quantities.
Multiply the A values together and add the powers of 10, then convert back to correct standard form if needed. E.g. (2 x 10^3) x (3 x 10^4) = 6 x 10^7.
Count digits from the first non-zero digit. 0.00450 has 3 significant figures (4, 5, 0). Leading zeros never count; trailing zeros after a decimal point do count.
Match your final answer to the significant figures of the least precise data given in the question, typically 2 or 3 sf at GCSE unless told otherwise.
Gradient = change in y / change in x, using two points far apart on the line for accuracy. On a distance-time graph this gives speed; on a velocity-time graph this gives acceleration.

For straight-line sections, split into rectangles and triangles and sum the areas. On a velocity-time graph, area = distance travelled; on a force-extension graph, area = work done/elastic potential energy.

items.term: Drawing a line/curve of best fit
items.detail: Draw a single smooth line that passes as close as possible to all points, with roughly equal numbers of points above and below; ignore clear anomalies when drawing the line but still plot them.
Percentage change = (change / original value) x 100. Used for efficiency, percentage uncertainty and comparing experimental to expected values.
For 'estimate' questions, round each value to 1 significant figure or the nearest convenient power of ten before calculating, and state the assumption made.

items.term: Direct and inverse proportion on graphs
items.detail: Direct proportion gives a straight line through the origin. Inverse proportion (e.g. pressure vs volume at constant temperature) gives a curve where P x V is constant - plotting P against 1/V gives a straight line through the origin instead.

1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks. Covers energy, electricity, particle model of matter, atomic structure. Aim for roughly 1 minute per mark, leaving 5-10 minutes to check calculations and units at the end.

1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks. Covers forces, waves, magnetism and electromagnetism, space physics. Aim for roughly 1 minute per mark; attempt all 6-mark and calculation questions even if unsure, as partial working earns marks.
Skim the whole paper, note which required practicals and equation-sheet topics appear, and start with the questions you are most confident on to bank early marks.
Check every calculation has correct units, every graph has labelled axes, and no multiple-choice question has been left blank.
Read all options before choosing, cross out options you know are wrong, and never leave a multiple choice question blank - a guess has a chance of being right.
Underline the command word (describe, explain, evaluate, calculate) in each question before writing, to avoid describing when an explanation is required or vice versa.

items.term: Using the mark allocation as a guide
items.detail: A question worth 3 marks needs roughly 3 distinct linked points; a 1-mark question needs a single short, precise answer - do not overwrite short-answer questions.
Always show the equation used, substitute with units, and every working step, even if unsure of the final answer, since method marks are awarded for correct working.

topics.name: P7.1 Magnetism and the Motor Effect
subtopics: Poles of a magnet, attraction and repulsion, and magnetic field patterns
Permanent magnets versus induced magnetism, and why induced magnetism is always attractive
Magnetic materials: iron, steel, cobalt, nickel
Using a plotting compass to map a field, and the Earths magnetic field as evidence of a magnetic core
Field around a straight current-carrying wire and the right-hand grip rule
Field of a solenoid, and how a soft iron core makes an electromagnet
The motor effect and the equation F equals B times I times l
Flemings left-hand rule: thumb motion, first finger field, second finger current
How a direct current electric motor works, including the role of the split-ring commutator
How a moving-coil loudspeaker converts variations in current into pressure variations

cards.front: State the equation for the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
cards.back: F equals B times I times l, where B is magnetic flux density in tesla, I is current in amps and l is length in metres.

cards.front: What does each finger represent in Flemings left-hand rule?
cards.back: Thumb is the direction of motion or force, first finger is the magnetic field from north to south, second finger is the conventional current.

cards.front: Why is induced magnetism always a force of attraction?
cards.back: The magnetic material develops poles aligned so that the nearest pole is opposite to the pole of the inducing magnet.

cards.front: What is the purpose of the split-ring commutator in a DC motor?
cards.back: It reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn so the coil keeps rotating in the same direction.

cards.front: How can the strength of an electromagnet be increased?
cards.back: Increase the current, increase the number of turns on the coil, or add or improve a soft iron core.

cards.front: What does the Earth having a magnetic field suggest about its core?
cards.back: That the core contains magnetic material and that the field is generated within the Earth.

cards.front: When is the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field zero?
cards.back: When the wire is parallel to the magnetic field lines.

cloze: The force on a conductor in a magnetic field is given by F = {{c1::BIl}}.
Magnetic flux density is measured in {{c1::tesla}}.
In Flemings left-hand rule the {{c1::thumb}} shows motion and the {{c2::second finger}} shows current.
A DC motor uses a {{c1::split-ring commutator}} to reverse the current every half turn.

topics.name: P7.3 Induced Potential, Generators and Transformers
subtopics: The generator effect: moving a conductor in a magnetic field induces a potential difference
How reversing the direction of motion or the field reverses the induced potential difference
How the induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the original change
The alternator producing alternating current using slip rings
The dynamo producing direct current using a split-ring commutator
How a microphone converts pressure variations into variations in current
Structure of a transformer: primary and secondary coils on an iron core
The transformer equation Vp over Vs equals np over ns
Power in an ideal transformer: Vp times Ip equals Vs times Is
Step-up transformers at the power station and step-down transformers near consumers
Why the National Grid transmits at high voltage and low current to reduce heating losses

cards.front: State the transformer turns equation.
cards.back: Potential difference across the primary over potential difference across the secondary equals number of primary turns over number of secondary turns.

cards.front: For a 100 percent efficient transformer, what is the power relationship?
cards.back: Vp times Ip equals Vs times Is - power in equals power out.

cards.front: Why does the National Grid use very high voltages?
cards.back: For a given power, higher voltage means lower current, and energy lost as heat in the cables depends on current squared, so losses are greatly reduced.

cards.front: What is the difference between an alternator and a dynamo?
cards.back: An alternator uses slip rings and generates alternating current; a dynamo uses a split-ring commutator and generates direct current.

cards.front: Give three ways to increase the induced potential difference in a generator.
cards.back: Move the conductor or coil faster, use a stronger magnetic field, or increase the number of turns on the coil.

cards.front: Why must a transformer be supplied with alternating current?
cards.back: A changing magnetic field is needed in the iron core to induce a potential difference in the secondary coil; direct current gives a constant field and no induction.

cards.front: How does a microphone work?
cards.back: Pressure variations in sound waves move a diaphragm attached to a coil in a magnetic field, inducing a varying current that represents the sound.

cloze: In an ideal transformer, {{c1::Vp times Ip}} equals {{c2::Vs times Is}}.
A {{c1::step-up}} transformer increases potential difference and has more turns on the {{c2::secondary}} coil.
The generator effect induces a potential difference when a conductor {{c1::moves}} relative to a magnetic field.
Transformers only work with {{c1::alternating}} current because a {{c2::changing}} magnetic field is needed.

topics.name: P4 Atomic Structure and Radioactivity
subtopics: Structure of the atom: radius 1 times 10 to the minus 10 metres, nucleus 1 times 10 to the minus 14 metres
Relative charges and masses of protons, neutrons and electrons
Atomic number, mass number, isotopes and ions
Electron energy levels, absorption and emission of electromagnetic radiation
Development of the model: plum pudding, Rutherford alpha scattering, Bohr, discovery of the neutron
Alpha, beta, gamma and neutron radiation: nature, penetration, ionising power
Writing nuclear decay equations and balancing mass and atomic numbers
Activity in becquerel, and the use of a Geiger-Muller tube
Half-life, and calculating net decline as a ratio
Contamination versus irradiation, and appropriate precautions
Hazards of radiation and the importance of peer review of findings
Background radiation sources and units of dose in sieverts
Uses of radiation: medical tracers, gamma therapy, sterilisation of instruments

cards.front: What is the approximate radius of an atom and of a nucleus?
cards.back: Atom about 1 times 10 to the minus 10 metres; nucleus about 1 times 10 to the minus 14 metres, roughly one ten-thousandth of the atom.

cards.front: What did the alpha particle scattering experiment show?
cards.back: That the mass of an atom is concentrated in a tiny positively charged nucleus with mostly empty space around it, replacing the plum pudding model.

cards.front: Compare the penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma.
cards.back: Alpha is stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air; beta is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium; gamma is only partly absorbed by thick lead or concrete.

cards.front: Which type of radiation is most strongly ionising?
cards.back: Alpha, because of its large mass and 2 plus charge - but it has the shortest range.

cards.front: Define half-life.
cards.back: The time taken for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample to halve, or for the activity or count rate to halve.

cards.front: What changes in the nucleus during beta decay?
cards.back: A neutron becomes a proton and a high-speed electron is emitted, so the mass number stays the same and the atomic number increases by 1.

cards.front: What changes in the nucleus during alpha decay?
cards.back: The nucleus emits two protons and two neutrons, so the mass number decreases by 4 and the atomic number by 2.

cards.front: Distinguish contamination from irradiation.
cards.back: Contamination is unwanted radioactive atoms being present on or in an object; irradiation is exposing an object to radiation without it becoming radioactive.

cards.front: What does gamma emission do to mass number and atomic number?
cards.back: Neither changes - gamma emission only removes energy from the nucleus.

cards.front: Why is peer review important for radiation research?
cards.back: Independent checking of published findings ensures conclusions are valid before the public and policymakers rely on them.

cloze: Alpha decay decreases the mass number by {{c1::4}} and the atomic number by {{c2::2}}.
Beta decay increases the atomic number by {{c1::1}} and leaves the mass number {{c2::unchanged}}.
Activity is measured in {{c1::becquerel}} and radiation dose in {{c2::sieverts}}.
{{c1::Contamination}} means unwanted radioactive atoms are on an object, whereas {{c2::irradiation}} does not make the object radioactive.

topics.name: P4.4 Nuclear Fission and Fusion
subtopics: Fission as the splitting of a large unstable nucleus, usually after absorbing a neutron
Products of fission: two smaller nuclei, two or three neutrons, and gamma rays
Energy released in fission and the chain reaction
Control rods absorbing neutrons, and the role of the moderator and coolant
The difference between a controlled chain reaction in a reactor and an uncontrolled one
Fusion as joining two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus
Why some mass is converted into energy during fusion
Conditions required for fusion: extremely high temperature and pressure
Why fusion is difficult to achieve on Earth
Comparing fission and fusion in terms of fuel, waste and conditions

cards.front: Define nuclear fission.
cards.back: The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei, usually after it absorbs a neutron, releasing energy plus two or three neutrons and gamma rays.

cards.front: What is a chain reaction?
cards.back: Neutrons released by one fission event go on to cause further fission events, so the reaction sustains itself.

cards.front: What do control rods do in a nuclear reactor?
cards.back: They absorb neutrons so the rate of fission can be controlled and kept steady.

cards.front: Define nuclear fusion.
cards.back: Two light nuclei joining to form a heavier nucleus, with some of the mass converted into energy released as radiation.

cards.front: Why does fusion require extremely high temperatures and pressures?
cards.back: Both nuclei are positively charged and repel each other, so enormous energy is needed to bring them close enough for fusion to occur.

cards.front: Compare the waste products of fission and fusion.
cards.back: Fission produces radioactive waste that needs long-term storage; fusion produces helium, with far less radioactive waste.

cloze: In a reactor, {{c1::control rods}} absorb neutrons to regulate the rate of fission.
Fusion joins two {{c1::light}} nuclei and converts some {{c2::mass}} into energy.
Fission usually starts when a large nucleus absorbs a {{c1::neutron}}.

topics.name: P8 Space Physics
subtopics: The solar system: the Sun, eight planets, dwarf planets, moons and artificial satellites
How a star forms from a nebula pulled together by gravity, becoming a protostar
Main sequence stability: outward radiation pressure balancing inward gravity
Life cycle of a star the size of the Sun: red giant, white dwarf
Life cycle of a star much larger than the Sun: red supergiant, supernova, neutron star or black hole
Fusion of hydrogen into helium and the formation of heavier elements up to iron in the core
How elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova and distributed
Orbital motion: gravity providing the centripetal force and changing direction not speed
Why a faster orbital speed is needed for a smaller radius orbit
Red-shift of light from distant galaxies and the evidence it provides
Why the observation that more distant galaxies recede faster supports the Big Bang
Dark mass and dark energy as current uncertainties

cards.front: What keeps a main sequence star stable?
cards.back: The outward pressure from energy released by fusion balances the inward force of gravity.

cards.front: Describe the life cycle of a star about the size of the Sun after the main sequence.
cards.back: It expands to a red giant, then the core contracts, shedding its outer layers to leave a white dwarf that cools.

cards.front: Describe the life cycle of a star much more massive than the Sun after the main sequence.
cards.back: It becomes a red supergiant, then explodes as a supernova, leaving either a neutron star or, if massive enough, a black hole.

cards.front: Where do elements heavier than iron come from?
cards.back: They are produced in a supernova explosion, which also distributes the elements through the universe.

cards.front: Why does an object in a circular orbit accelerate even at constant speed?
cards.back: Its direction is constantly changing, so its velocity changes; gravity provides the centripetal force causing this acceleration.

cards.front: What is red-shift and what does it tell us?
cards.back: Light from receding galaxies has its wavelength increased towards the red end of the spectrum; the greater the red-shift, the faster the galaxy is moving away, which supports an expanding universe.

cards.front: What happens to the orbital speed needed if the orbital radius decreases?
cards.back: A greater orbital speed is required for a stable orbit at a smaller radius.

cards.front: What is a protostar?
cards.back: A cloud of dust and gas pulled together by gravity, heating up as it contracts until fusion begins.

cloze: A star forms from a {{c1::nebula}} of dust and gas pulled together by {{c2::gravity}}.
A star the size of the Sun ends as a {{c1::white dwarf}} after a red giant stage.
Elements heavier than {{c1::iron}} are formed in a {{c2::supernova}}.
{{c1::Red-shift}} of distant galaxies provides evidence for the {{c2::Big Bang}} theory.

subtopics: Density equals mass over volume, and required practical for regular and irregular solids and liquids
Particle model explanations of the differences between solids, liquids and gases
Internal energy as the total kinetic and potential energy of the particles
Specific heat capacity, E equals m c delta theta, and the required practical
Specific latent heat of fusion and of vaporisation, E equals m L
Heating and cooling graphs and why temperature is constant during a change of state
Conservation of mass during changes of state and why they are physical not chemical changes
Gas pressure from particle collisions with container walls

cards.front: State the equation for specific heat capacity.
cards.back: Change in thermal energy equals mass times specific heat capacity times change in temperature.

cards.front: Define specific latent heat.
cards.back: The energy required to change the state of one kilogram of a substance with no change in temperature.

cards.front: Why is temperature constant during a change of state?
cards.back: The energy supplied is used to break the bonds between particles rather than to increase their kinetic energy.

cards.front: State the equation for density.
cards.back: Density equals mass divided by volume.

cards.front: State the equation for pressure in a column of liquid.
cards.back: Pressure equals height of the column times density of the liquid times gravitational field strength.

cards.front: Explain how a gas exerts pressure on its container.
cards.back: Particles move randomly and collide with the container walls, each collision exerting a force; pressure is the total force per unit area.

cards.front: What happens to the pressure of a fixed mass of gas if its temperature rises at constant volume?
cards.back: Pressure increases, because the particles move faster and collide with the walls more often and more forcefully.

cards.front: Why does atmospheric pressure decrease with altitude?
cards.back: There are fewer air molecules above, so the weight of air acting on a given area is lower, and the atmosphere is also less dense at higher altitude.

cards.front: What is upthrust and when does an object float?
cards.back: Upthrust is the upward force from a fluid due to the pressure difference between the bottom and top of an object; it floats when upthrust equals its weight.

cards.front: How does doing work on a gas by compression affect its temperature?
cards.back: Work done transfers energy to the internal energy store of the gas, so its temperature increases.

cloze: Change in thermal energy equals mass times {{c1::specific heat capacity}} times change in {{c2::temperature}}.
Pressure in a column of liquid equals {{c1::h}} times {{c2::rho}} times g.
During a change of state, energy is used to break {{c1::bonds}} rather than raise {{c2::temperature}}.
Density equals {{c1::mass}} divided by {{c2::volume}}.

cards.front: Give the equation linking work done, force and distance.
cards.back: Work done equals force times distance moved along the line of action of the force.

cards.front: State the equation for kinetic energy.
cards.back: Kinetic energy equals one half times mass times speed squared.

cards.front: State the equation for gravitational potential energy.
cards.back: Gravitational potential energy equals mass times gravitational field strength times change in height.

cards.front: State the equation linking power, energy and time.
cards.back: Power equals energy transferred divided by time.

cards.front: State the equation for electrical power in terms of current and resistance.
cards.back: Power equals current squared times resistance.

cards.front: What is the difference between accuracy and precision?
cards.back: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value; precision is how closely repeated measurements agree with each other.

cards.front: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
cards.back: The distance travelled.

cards.front: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph represent?
cards.back: Speed.

cards.front: Difference between the command words describe and explain?
cards.back: Describe asks what happens; explain asks why it happens, requiring reasoning or a causal mechanism.

cloze: Kinetic energy equals {{c1::one half}} times mass times {{c2::speed squared}}.
